headline: Comfortable retirement costs rising faster than inflation due to utilities, healthcare and personal care expenses, widening the gap versus a modest retirement
reasoning: ASFA research shows that costs forming a big part of retiree budgets — particularly electricity, healthcare and personal care — are rising faster than general inflation. This means retirees seeking a comfortable (rather than modest) standard of living need larger superannuation balances to supplement any age pension entitlement. Modest retirement costs remain relatively well supported by the age pension, which is indexed to inflation, but comfortable retirement is becoming progressively more expensive in real terms.
quote: When you look at retirees who want to have more than just a modest standard of living and want to actually have a comfortable retirement, those retirees are finding that it's actually becoming more expensive. And the reason for that is because the kind of costs that form a big part of retiree budgets. So things like utilities and particularly electricity, but also healthcare, personal care and so on, all of those costs are actually rising faster than inflation, which means that in order for a retiree to have a comfortable standard of living in retirement, they need to have more in their superannuation to supplement any age pension entitlement that they might have to maintain that standard of living.
episode_title: Why a comfortable retirement is now costing more | the advisory

headline: Early super access debate: withdrawing even small amounts early has a magnified negative compounding effect over a decades-long working life; systemic policy response needed beyond super alone
reasoning: Philip Marquet notes existing compassionate grounds already allow early access to superannuation under tight constraints such as imminent risk of losing one's home or serious medical conditions, but warns that even small early withdrawals have a magnified negative effect on retirement balances through compounding over decades. He acknowledges the genuine financial insecurity many young Australians face when starting families or buying homes but argues the superannuation system alone cannot solve those pressures and a more holistic policy response is needed.
quote: We know that even withdrawing small amounts from your super earlier in your working life will have a magnified effect later in life through the nature of compounding over the course of what might be, you know, decades long working life. I do think though, there is a broader issue here around the fact that many young people do feel like their greatest financial insecurity will come at some of those earlier stages of life, you know, when you're when you're starting a family, when you're buying a house and so on. I'm not sure though that the solution to those problems can be solely addressed by the superannuation system alone. I think there there needs to be a more holistic policy response to those kind of pressures.
episode_title: Why a comfortable retirement is now costing more | the advisory

headline: APRA performance test working: members in underperforming super products fell from ~1 million five years ago to ~4,500 today, with failing funds improving returns, cutting fees or transferring members
reasoning: APRA's annual performance test covers most superannuation products and measures returns against a series of benchmarks. In the latest round, one MySuper product and eleven choice products failed. When the test was first introduced approximately five years ago, around one million members were in underperforming products; that figure has now fallen to roughly 4,500, indicating the regime is achieving its objective. Products that previously failed have generally either transferred members to better-performing vehicles, improved investment performance, or lowered fees.
quote: There was one my super product which failed the test. That's the the low cost simple option that you're defaulted into if you haven't made a choice about where you want your super to go. And there were eleven choice products that failed the test. That's a much smaller pool of underperforming products. When the test was first introduced about five years ago, there was something like a million members across the country who were invested in underperforming super products. On the latest test, those numbers are now down to about four and a half thousand. So that's so. A huge reduction. An indication this is actually working. I think that's right. And we have seen that those products that have failed the test in previous years have generally either transferred their members into better performing products or have taken steps to either improve their investment performance or lower their fees so that members have the benefit of better overall returns.
episode_title: Why a comfortable retirement is now costing more | the advisory

headline: APRA raises geopolitical risk alert for the superannuation sector, urging funds to ensure existing risk management frameworks are adequate for the current environment
reasoning: Marquet notes that APRA recently wrote to the financial services industry about heightened geopolitical risk and its potential impact on superannuation specifically. While geopolitical risk is not a new concern for the industry, APRA's focus is now on ensuring that existing risk assessment and risk management measures within super funds are sufficient given the increasingly complex global environment in recent years.
quote: Apra wrote a letter to the financial services industry at large a few weeks ago, talking about heightened geopolitical risk and the way it could impact the financial services sector generally, but also superannuation specifically. Now this is nothing new. The industry has known about geopolitical risk for a very long time, and we've all seen that geopolitical risk has increased in recent years. I think what APRA is more concerned about now is making sure that some of the existing risk assessment and risk management measures that super funds have in place to deal with...
episode_title: Why super's biggest test is changing | the advisory

headline: Australian superannuation performance test risks incentivising benchmark-hugging rather than outperformance, prompting a government review of the framework
reasoning: Marquet explains that the super performance test has successfully weeded out underperforming funds since its introduction, but its design may now be creating perverse incentives. Funds facing serious consequences for failing the test may shift from chasing outperformance to simply minimising the risk of failing, which could mean more index-hugging behaviour. The government's consultation paper is exploring changes to how novel or illiquid assets — such as student accommodation, renewable energy, infrastructure and venture capital — are benchmarked, given these do not correlate well with existing indices. One proposal is to move to a simpler CPI-plus benchmark for such assets. A separate, more complex proposal involves measuring risk-adjusted performance, though Marquet flags this would be very difficult to implement fairly across diverse fund strategies.
quote: The concern, though, that the government has, which has been raised by industry for quite a while, is that the way the performance test is calibrated could have an impact on the way that super funds are investing. So when you tell super funds that they might face significant consequences for failing the performance test, you create a risk that funds might no longer be chasing outperformance and might simply be investing in a way that is designed to minimise the risk of failing the performance test.
episode_title: Why super's biggest test is changing | the advisory

headline: ASIC scrutiny of platform trustees intensifies following Shield and First Guardian collapses, raising concerns about member risk exposure in self-directed super strategies
reasoning: Marquet highlights that the platform trustee model — which allows members to construct their own investment strategies from a large menu of options, often with adviser help — is very difficult to fit within existing superannuation performance measures. The collapse of Shield and First Guardian schemes exposed how members on platforms can be exposed to significant risk when chosen products fail. ASIC is releasing a report into how platform trustees are monitoring retirement risks, reflecting growing regulatory attention on this part of the industry.
quote: The issue around platform trustees has become a much more live issue since the collapse of the Shield and First Guardian schemes, which were offered on a range of superannuation platforms. A platform in the super industry functions a bit like a menu for your superannuation investment strategy. An individual, perhaps with the help of their advisor, can pick and choose which investments they want to include in their investment strategy from a menu of hundreds or thousands of different investment options. Now, what is very difficult about that platform model is fitting it within the existing performance measures that we have in the superannuation industry.
episode_title: Why super's biggest test is changing | the advisory

headline: Super fund benchmarking proposals could unlock greater allocation to infrastructure, renewables and venture capital by replacing ill-fitting indices with a CPI-plus measure
reasoning: Marquet notes that the existing performance test benchmarks work well for liquid listed assets like ASX equities but poorly for alternative investments including student accommodation, renewable energy, infrastructure, and emerging venture capital. Because no clear benchmark exists for these asset classes, funds may be discouraged from allocating to them under the current regime. The proposed shift to a CPI-plus benchmark for such assets is intended to remove this disincentive and allow super funds to invest more freely in productive, longer-duration assets.
quote: One of the proposed changes is to move to a new, simpler CPI plus benchmark for those kind of assets that don't correlate particularly well to any of the existing indices. All right. Because I guess much as maybe was designed when the majority of the bulk of super assets were just shares really, weren't they? That's right. But now, of course, we've got the diversity of assets that they can invest in.
episode_title: Why super's biggest test is changing | the advisory
